intro:
1 Kings opens with King David old and cold—they bring virgin Abishag to warm him but 'the king knew her not.' Meanwhile, his son Adonijah throws a coronation party: 'I will be king!' He invites all his brothers except Solomon, and all officials except Nathan the prophet and Zadok the priest.

Nathan and Bathsheba do a tag-team intervention: Bathsheba tells David about Adonijah's coup, Nathan confirms. David, though feeble, activates: 'Call Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah. Put Solomon on my mule, anoint him king at Gihon.' They do it immediately—trumpets blowing, people cheering so loud Adonijah's party hears it. Guests scatter, Adonijah clings to altar horns begging mercy. Solomon spares him conditionally.

David's final charge to Solomon: 'Be strong, keep God's commands. Also... deal with Joab (killed Abner and Amasa) and Shimei (cursed me).' David dies after 40-year reign.

Solomon establishes rule: executes Adonijah (asks for Abishag as wife—political move), exiles Abiathar priest, executes Joab at altar, tells Shimei 'Stay in Jerusalem or die'—Shimei leaves to retrieve slaves, gets executed.

God appears to Solomon in dream: 'Ask what I shall give you.' Solomon asks for wisdom to govern. God's pleased: gives wisdom PLUS riches, honor, long life if obedient. Famous judgment: two women claim same baby, Solomon says 'Cut it in half,' real mother reveals herself.

Solomon's reign peaks: builds temple in 7 years (cedar from Lebanon, gold everywhere), then his own palace in 13 years. Temple dedication: glory cloud fills it, Solomon prays epic dedication. God appears again: 'If you or people sin but repent, I'll hear.'

Solomon's wisdom becomes global brand: queen of Sheba visits, overwhelmed by his wealth and wisdom. 700 wives, 300 concubines—many foreign, bringing their gods. In old age, Solomon's heart turns to Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh. God warns: kingdom will tear away, but for David's sake not in your lifetime.

Enter Jeroboam: Solomon's official, prophet Ahijah tears new cloak into 12 pieces, gives him 10: 'God will tear kingdom from Solomon's son, give you 10 tribes.' Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt.

Solomon dies after 40-year reign. His son Rehoboam takes throne. People ask: 'Lighten your father's heavy yoke.' Rehoboam consults elders: 'Serve them.' Consults young friends: 'Tell them my pinky thicker than my father's thigh. Scorpions instead of whips.'

Result: Israel rebels: 'To your tents, O Israel!' Only Judah stays with Rehoboam. Kingdom splits: North=Israel (10 tribes, Jeroboam king), South=Judah (Rehoboam). Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Dan and Bethel: 'Too much trouble going to Jerusalem.' Establishes rival priesthood, festivals.

Rest of 1 Kings alternates between northern and southern kings. Northern kings all evil, southern kings mixed. Elijah appears dramatically: tells Ahab 'No dew or rain except by my word.' Fed by ravens, then widow of Zarephath whose flour and oil don't run out, raises her son from dead.

Mount Carmel showdown: 450 Baal prophets vs. Elijah alone. 'How long will you limp between two opinions?' Baal prophets cut themselves, no fire. Elijah soaks altar with water, prays, fire falls from heaven. People shout 'The Lord, He is God!' Kill Baal prophets. Rain returns.

Elijah flees Jezebel's threat, meets God at Horeb in whisper, not wind/earthquake/fire. Anoints Elisha as successor.

Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard, Jezebel arranges Naboth's murder. Elijah confronts: 'Dogs will lick your blood where they licked Naboth's.' Ahab temporarily repents, judgment delayed.

Book ends with Ahab's death in battle (prophesied), Judah's king Jehoshaphat's reforms, and Ahaziah (Ahab's son) taking throne in Israel.
outro:
1 Kings closes with the divided kingdom in full swing. The once-united Israel under David and Solomon is now two rival nations with competing worship centers—Jerusalem vs. Dan/Bethel.

Major themes:
1. **The temple tension** – Solomon builds glorious temple but his heart turns to foreign gods. Physical building ≠ spiritual faithfulness.
2. **Wisdom's limits** – Solomon had supernatural wisdom but still made disastrous personal choices. Knowledge ≠ obedience.
3. **Division consequences** – Kingdom splits not just politically but religiously. Jeroboam's 'convenient' worship leads to centuries of idolatry.
4. **Prophetic confrontation** – Elijah vs. Baal prophets shows God's power amidst national apostasy.
5. **Leadership legacy** – Solomon starts well, ends compromised. His spiritual decline affects millions.

The Elijah narratives inject hope: even when kings fail, God raises up prophetic voices. The Mount Carmel showdown remains one of the Bible's most dramatic faith demonstrations.

Historical note: The split wasn't just Rehoboam's arrogance—tribal tensions existed since David's time, Solomon's oppressive labor policies fueled resentment.

Looking forward: 2 Kings continues the sad decline of both kingdoms toward exile. Elijah passes mantle to Elisha, northern kings get worse, occasional southern reforms delay judgment.

The book leaves us with divided loyalty—a physical picture of spiritual divided hearts. The need for a true Son of David who can reunite God's people becomes clearer.
